newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel-PLO talks stagnate, violence brews.
newsitem.headline: Israel-PLO talks stagnate, violence brews.

text.p: Clashes with Palestinians and the threat of war with Syria provide grim backdrop for Israel's talks with the PLO on a partial withdrawal from the West Bank town of Hebron with an agreement still out of reach.
Israeli and Palestinian leaders said after talks on Tuesday they were still determined to reach a deal but there was no sign they had narrowed their differences.
In Jerusalem, thousands of right-wing Israelis rallied to block any agreement, blasting U.S. mediation efforts as a pressure tool on Israel.

"We hope the government will stay strong and have the courage not to turn over parts of the city of our fathers to the hands of terrorists," said Dov Lior, rabbi of the Kiryat Arba settlement near Hebron.

Hebron, where 400 Jews live among 100,000 Arabs, was again a flashpoint of violence on Tuesday as settlers shouting "Hebron is ours" shoved, cursed and spat at PLO officials who toured the city, Arab and Israeli witnesses said.
Israel promised in a peace deal last year to give Palestinians control of parts of Hebron, where tombs of biblical forefathers are held holy by both Moslems and Jews.
Hebron is the last of seven West Bank towns Israel agreed to hand over for Palestinian self-rule under peace deals negotiated by the previous Labour government.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who ousted Labour in elections last May, opposed the peace deals but has vowed to honour the Hebron redeployment once Palestinians agree to modifications aimed at safeguarding Jewish settlers in the town.
Palestinians have refused to reopen the 1995 deal which envisaged an Israeli Hebron withdrawal by last March.
Violence also erupted in a West Bank village after the funeral of a 10-year-old Palestinian boy who relatives said had been killed by a Jewish settler on Sunday.
Israeli soldiers clashed with Palestinian stone-throwers in the village in scenes reminiscent of a six-year Palestinian uprising that preceded the landmark 1993 Israel-PLO peace deal.
Other Israeli troops on Tuesday ended a large military exercise in the Golan Heights amid mounting tension with neighbouring Syria.

An Israeli army spokesman said the manoeuvres, which involved warplanes, tanks and artillery units, were "routine" and had been planned in advance, much the way Syria described a series of military exercises on its side of the border.

Syrian Foreign Minister Farouq al-Shara denied on Tuesday that Damascus was planning a surprise attack against Israel, and the United States said widescale Syrian troop movements in Lebanon were not a cause for concern, but anxiety in Israel remained high.
"Allegations...that Syria is escalating the situation and massing troops to launch a surprise attack are baseless," Shara said in Damascus.
"Such allegations coming from the Israeli government are aimed at evading the peace process and the basis on which it was built," he told reporters.
Syria and Israel have already fought several wars and have failed in five years of sporadic peace talks to settle their dispute over the fate of the Golan Heights which Israel captured in 1967.
Syria wants back all of the Golan, a high-altitude plateau, in exchange for peace. Netanyahu has vowed never to give up the strategic heights.
